title: Social Media Messaging, Fake News, and COVID-19 outbreak in Lagos, Nigeria
screen_reason: Cross-sectional online survey of 259 Lagos residents reporting the share of respondents who say they have read fake news about COVID-19 on social media (Table 1: 39.6% very large extent, 43.5% large extent; text reports 83.1% combined). Self-reported encounter with misinformation with a stated denominator = RECALL (exposure).

estimates.platform: social media (Facebook, Twitter, WhatsApp, Instagram named in the paper's framing)
estimates.date: not stated; article received 7 Feb 2022, published 2022
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they have read fake news about COVID-19 on social media to a large or very large extent
estimates.denominator: 259 adult residents of Lagos State, Nigeria, recruited by purposive sampling to an online (Google Form) questionnaire
estimates.definition: Respondent answered 'very large extent' or 'large extent' to the item 'I have read fake news on social media about COVID-19'
estimates.misinfo_def: "scholars agree that fake news can be regarded as a deliberate effort to mislead individuals"; fake news classified into "(i) disinformation, (ii) propaganda, (iii) hoaxes, (iv) satire/parody, (v) inaccuracies in journalism, and (vi) partisanship"
estimates.source_quote: In addition, the table shows that 83.1% of the respondents were adequately aware of fake news reports on social media about COVID-19 outbreak, while less than 14% of the respondents were inadequately aware of fake news reports on social media about COVID-19 outbreak.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-classification; no external verification. Closed-ended Likert item on an online Google Form questionnaire; no coder reliability reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: The sampling technique adopted for this study was purposive sampling technique. This is because this study was concerned with the variability of the data during the pandemic. The criteria for the purposive sampling were: 1. The respondents must be a resident in Lagos State. 2. The respondent must be a Nigerian citizen. 3. The respondent must be ICT savvy. The instrument used for data collection was the online questionnaire.
estimates.notes: The 83.1% figure is stated verbatim in both the abstract and the Results, and equals the two top Likert categories of the Table 1 item; it is the paper's headline number, so kept under R8 (verbatim). Data-collection dates are never given; year set to the publication year. Platform coded multi_platform because the item asks about 'social media' in general, not one service.

missed_or_uncertain: Table 2 items were not extracted: 'I have cautioned individuals about fake news on COVID-19 in social media' (36.2% strongly agree + 30.3% agree; the text reports 'almost 67%'), 'I have been warned to detect and avoid fake news report on COVID-19' (54%), and 'I have been engaged in debates about fake news reports on group chats' (48.3% + 18.2%). None of these is exposure to, or sharing of, misinformation - they are corrective/warning behaviours and discussion about fake news, so they fall outside all six included constructs. Table 1 columns 'I have heard of COVID-19' (99.6%) and 'I have read social media report on COVID-19' (almost 92%) are exposure to COVID-19 information in general, not to misinformation, so they were not extracted. The 3.1% 'Never' cell would imply 96.9% encountered at least some fake news, but that is a complement I would have to compute, which R8 forbids. The 70 fake-news reports analysed by Neto et al. in Brazil (>50% about statements of health authorities) are cited from another paper, not this study's data.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online questionnaire (Google Form), purposive sample of 259 Lagos State residents screened on residence, Nigerian citizenship and being 'ICT savvy'; population framed as 20 million Lagos residents. No response rate, no fieldwork dates, no questionnaire validation, no coder or scale reliability statistics reported. Ethnographic observation is reported qualitatively only. Analysis is descriptive percentages plus a Spearman correlation and Somers' D.
rob.item6_quote: Interestingly, scholars agree that fake news can be regarded as a deliberate effort to mislead individuals. Furthermore, fake news may have commercial, non-commercial and professional forms (Bharali & Goswami, 2018; Reilly, 2012).
rob.item10_quote: In addition, the table shows that 83.1% of the respondents were adequately aware of fake news reports on social media about COVID-19 outbreak, while less than 14% of the respondents were inadequately aware of fake news reports on social media about COVID-19 outbreak.
